# Top 5 tools for a founders' decision ledger

Source: https://lowob.com/research/top-5-tools-for-a-founders-decision-ledger/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-21 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: None of these tools is truly append-only. Every one lets someone edit an old entry. What matters is how long the tool keeps history, whether you can get everything out in an open format, and whether it is easy enough that the weekly habit survives. Notion ranks first for flexibility and AI drafting, followed by Slite, Airtable, Obsidian and Tana. A shared document and a 30-minute weekly review beat a perfect database nobody opens.

## Key points

- This list is for founding teams of two to fifty people who want one shared record of what they decided, why, and what would change their minds. If you already keep decisions somewhere and read them, the tool matters far less than the habit.
- Notion keeps page history for 7 days on Free, 30 on Plus, 90 on Business and without limit only on Enterprise, so an edited entry can lose its original wording.
- Airtable keeps revision and snapshot history for one year on its Team and Business plans and two weeks on Free.
- Obsidian stores every entry as a Markdown file on your own machine; the app is free and a commercial licence is $50 per user a year.
- Never edit an old entry. Add a new one that supersedes it, and link the two.

A decision ledger is the simplest form of what our explainer on [decision records](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) describes: one entry per decision, with the reason, the owner, the alternatives rejected and the outcome you expect. The idea is older than any of these tools. Michael Nygard named the architecture decision record in 2011, and Martin Fowler's summary states the rule that matters most here: a record "should never be reopened or changed - instead it should be superseded". **lowob**'s piece [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) argues the same for commercial decisions. No tool on this list enforces that rule, so the ranking is about how well each one lets you see what an entry said on the day it was written.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Version history | 30% | You need to see what an entry said when the decision was made, not after someone tidied it. |
| Open export | 25% | The record should outlive the tool. |
| Ease of the weekly habit | 25% | The ledger only works if people write in it within the hour. |
| AI drafting and price | 20% | Drafting entries from calls and memos makes capture cheap. |

## The list

**1. Notion**

**Best for:** teams that want a database of decisions with views by owner, date and status, plus AI drafting.

**Why it ranks first:** flexible enough to hold a proper decision record (decision, reason, what would prove it wrong, review date, outcome) and easy enough that people use it. A database of decisions can be filtered by owner and sorted by review date, which turns the weekly review into a single view. Custom agents can draft entries from meeting notes and memos.

**Watch out for:** page history is 7 days on Free, 30 on Plus, 90 on Business and unlimited only on Enterprise. On the cheaper plans, an entry edited three months after the decision can lose its original wording for good. Agents run on paid credits, at $10 per 1,000 credits after a free trial.

**Pricing:** Free; Plus $10 per member a month billed annually ($12 monthly); Business $20 ($24 monthly); Enterprise custom (as listed in October and November 2026, per a third-party snapshot of Notion's pricing page).

**What would change its rank:** longer history on cheaper tiers, or a locking feature for past entries.

**2. Slite**

**Best for:** teams that want a clear record of who and what changed an entry.

**Why it ranks here:** its June 2026 update made the activity log record where every edit came from, whether the app, the API, MCP or Slite's own agent, with three months of history backfilled. That matters more as agents start writing into the ledger: you can tell a person's edit from a machine's. MCP access is now included on all plans, including Basic, so an agent can read and draft entries.

**Watch out for:** a smaller vendor, less flexible than a database, and we could not confirm version history limits or security certification by tier on Slite's pages this month.

**Pricing:** Basic $10 per user a month billed annually ($12 monthly); Pro $20 ($25 monthly); Enterprise custom (as listed in November 2026, per a pricing tracker's snapshot of Slite's page). There is no free tier, only a 14-day trial.

**What would change its rank:** structured fields for falsifiers and review dates.

**3. Airtable**

**Best for:** teams that want a strict, structured ledger with required fields and linked records.

**Why it ranks here:** the most rigorous structure: every decision is a row, with required fields, links to evidence and views for review dates. Revision and snapshot history run for a year on Team and Business, which covers a full cycle of quarterly reviews. Read-only collaborators are not billed, so the whole company can read the ledger while only the people who write in it pay.

**Watch out for:** expensive for what a small team needs, and a year of history is not forever. Export the base before the year runs out on decisions you expect to revisit.

**Pricing:** Free with two weeks of history; Team $20 per collaborator a month billed annually ($24 monthly); Business $45 ($54 monthly); Enterprise Scale through sales (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** history longer than a year on the Team plan.

**4. Obsidian**

**Best for:** founders who want plain files they own outright.

**Why it ranks here:** the best answer on ownership: every decision is a Markdown file on your machine, readable by anything, for as long as the file exists. The app is "free without limits". Paid Sync adds version history across devices. Because files are plain text, you can also put the folder under version control, which gives you a permanent history of every change.

**Watch out for:** weak team permissions and no built-in AI, so it suits two founders better than twenty people. Obsidian's pricing page does not state how long Sync keeps version history; check before you rely on it.

**Pricing:** app free; commercial licence $50 per user a year; Sync $4 per user a month billed annually ($5 monthly) (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** better team sharing.

**5. Tana**

**Best for:** founders who think in outlines and want an AI meeting agent feeding the ledger.

**Why it ranks here:** an outliner with structure and a botless meeting companion for Zoom, Teams and Google Meet on every plan, so decisions can flow from calls into structured records. Tana lists SOC 2 Type 2 on all tiers.

**Watch out for:** a steep learning curve for new team members, which works against the weekly habit.

**Pricing:** Free; Pro $15 per member a month billed yearly; Business custom (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** an easier start for new team members.

## Side by side

|  | Notion | Slite | Airtable | Obsidian | Tana |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shape of the ledger | Database with views | Documents | Strict table with required fields | Markdown files | Structured outline |
| History on entry paid plan | 30 days (Plus) | Edit-source log; limits not verified | 1 year (Team) | Sync history; length not stated | Not verified |
| History on free plan | 7 days | No free plan | 2 weeks | Local files only | Not verified |
| Open export | Not verified this month | API and MCP | Not verified this month | Plain files you hold | Not verified |
| AI drafting | Custom agents on credits | Slite agent; MCP | Not ranked on AI | None built in | Botless meeting agent |
| Entry paid price, November 2026 | $10 a member a month, annual | $10 a user a month, annual | $20 a collaborator a month, annual | $50 a user a year licence | $15 a member a month, annual |

> The tool cannot stop someone editing an old entry. Only the rule can: never edit, always supersede.

## Left out, and why

**Google Docs.** The simplest option and often the right one for two founders. Not ranked because it has no structure, but a single shared document with a weekly review is a perfectly good ledger.

**Coda.** We could not confirm its current plans and direction on its own pages this month.

**Linear, Confluence and Attio.** An issue tracker, a heavyweight wiki and a CRM: each can hold decisions, none is built for it.

## A template that works in any of them

| Field | What goes in it |
| --- | --- |
| Date and decision | One line |
| Why | One or two sentences |
| Rejected | The alternatives you did not choose |
| What would prove it wrong | The signal, and the date to check it |
| Who disagreed | Their name and what they predicted |
| Outcome | Filled in on the check date |
| Supersedes | A link to the entry this one replaces, if any |

Never edit an old entry. Add a new one that supersedes it, and link the two. The field list follows the architecture decision record format, which Fowler describes as the decision, its context, the alternatives and the consequences, adapted for commercial decisions. Our piece on [the field that makes a record a judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/) explains why "what would prove it wrong" is the one to protect, and our piece on [the founders' ledger](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/) covers how the habit starts with two people.

## lowob takeaways

- **Notion ranks first for flexibility.** But its page history is 7 to 90 days below Enterprise, so the supersede rule matters most there.
- **Airtable keeps a year.** One year of revision history on Team and Business, and readers are free.
- **Obsidian wins on ownership.** Plain Markdown files on your machine, readable by anything.
- **The rule beats the tool.** Never edit an old entry; supersede it and link the two.

Gateway card

### Buyer's checklist for a decision ledger tool

- You know how long the plan you will actually buy keeps history
- An entry can be exported in an open format and read without the tool
- Writing an entry takes less than five minutes
- Each entry has a reason, an owner, a falsifier and a review date
- Superseding entries link to the ones they replace
- A weekly 30-minute review is in the calendar before the tool is bought

## Common questions

### What is the best tool for keeping a startup decision log?

This list ranks Notion first for flexibility and AI drafting, followed by Slite, Airtable, Obsidian and Tana. The habit matters more than the tool, and a shared document with a weekly review is a perfectly good ledger for two founders.

### How long does Notion keep page history?

As listed in October 2026, 7 days on Free, 30 on Plus, 90 on Business and unlimited only on Enterprise, so an edited entry can lose its original wording on cheaper plans.

### What should a decision log entry include?

The date and decision in one line, why, what was rejected, what would prove it wrong and when to check, who disagreed and what they predicted, and the outcome on the check date, plus a link to any entry it supersedes.

### Should you edit old entries in a decision log?

No. The architecture decision record practice is that an accepted record is never changed but superseded by a new one that links back, so the log shows what was believed at the time.
